#9919. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

In some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

For example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually says the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

To build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11

Within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister."

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

Other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to new audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

#9918. Free e-government platform that serves two billion people in ten countries has critical SQL injection bug

India’s Digital Infrastructure for Governance Impact and Transformation tool can leak data

India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens.

The platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection. Third party developers can also create DIGIT modules, and plenty have done so and now offer add-ons that handle tasks as diverse as managing birth and death certificates, revenue collection, and running water treatment plants.

DIGIT is ubiquitous in India, where all state and union territory governments use the platform, as do over 20,000 local government entities.

India also exports DIGIT under its policy of turning software created for its own needs into “digital public goods” (DPI) that it happily gives away to other nations. Nine nations have implemented DIGIT to some degree, among them Mozambique, Liberia, Senegal, Nigeria, Burundi, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Jamaica, and Sri Lanka

India’s population is 1.4 billion. Indonesia’s is 280 million and Nigeria is home to 240 million. DIGIT is therefore used by governments that serve over two billion people, some of whom are now at risk thanks to CVE-2026-136706, a 9.3-rated SQL injection flaw present in DIGIT which allows “improper neutralization of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected User and Access Control Service components.”

“An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to CERT-IN. “Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized disclosure, modification or deletion of database information on the targeted system.”

eGov India, which oversees work on DIGIT, has released source code for an update that fixes the problem.

While local government users of DIGIT typically access it as SaaS, through large implementations run by national or state governments, over 1,000 deployments are live across various cities and other entities.

Those orgs can therefore add patching DIGIT to their urgent to-do lists, along with fixing Java, PHP, vCenter and any other widely used technologies that suddenly need an urgent security update. ®

A bit like credit card companies your payments to them are an asset, but your debt to them (most of which is actually just virtual on a balance sheet) is also a commodity they they can roll into financial instruments and profit from. For those who never heard of con artists, "circular financing" is the idea that I give you one dollar, on condition that you give it straight back to me.Not quite. Note that I don't just give the dollar back to you: I use it to buy your merch.(3) You remain with $1 invested in my company, and you can claim $1 in revenue from the sale, but you are out $1 worth of inventory. No. Nobody magically "made" a dollar. It's just a financial trick that lets you effectively buy equity in my company with your product. It's a good arrangement as long as my company grows in value, and thus adds to the value of the assets on your balance-sheet.

Well, sort of they do... Sadly, you have to make a more complex description:

1) You invest $10 in my company, on condition of (2)2) I use that $10 to buy your product. You make $10 of revenue, and $2 of profit on that transaction (let's assume $0 of operating costs, just to keep it simple)3) I still owe you $10, which you put down as an asset4) Your calculated company value goes up. Let's say you have a "value multiplier" of 10. Had you not made the sale, you'd have $10 of assets, $0 of revenue, and $0 of profit. Your company value would be $0 (profit based) or $0 (revenue based), and at best $10 (asset based). However, after the sale, you have a value of $20 (profit based) or $100 (revenue based). The $10 of assets don't really count here as it's already baked into the value (it's complicated, don't worry about it).

In a publicly traded company, that valuation change means your share price will go up. Shareholders therefore make some paper money until they cash out for actual money. Good for the shareholders. However, the company can issue new shares are the higher price to get money for... more circular financing.

There's a multiplying force if my company grows too. It means I no longer owe you $10, instead I owe you $20 - which is still an asset on your books. In the above example, it could mean your multiplier goes from 10 to 11 or something, which again, bumps your share price up (and around we go all over again).

Maybe not a chapter 11 type event, but a firing 80% of the workforce type event. Ultimately, nvidia still makes things people want, and whilst the market for those things may dramatically shrink for several years, we still need someone to sell us GPUs, just maybe not in the volumes they've been used to of late. Hence my thinking it won't collapse entirely, but we'll see.

There is probably a bubble. It will probably "pop." Stock prices will collapse, some companies will disappear, and others will consolidate. Ten years from now, I suspect today's AI economy will be a fraction of what it has become.

The Railroad Bubble (The Panic of 1873)All the steel rails! 35,000 miles! Dark railways...

Between 1866 and 1873, America laid 35,000 miles of new railroad track. The ensuing financial crisis drove roughly a quarter of the nation's 364 railroad companies into bankruptcy. Jay Cooke & Company's bankruptcy, precipitated by its investment in the Northern Pacific Railway, triggered the panic.

Railroad magnates and financiers acquired distressed railroads, reorganized them, and consolidated their operations. The resulting national logistics network helped fuel the American Industrial Revolution and enabled businesses like Sears Roebuck, Standard Oil, and US Steel to operate at unprecedented scales.

The railroad bubble burst. Railroads did not become irrelevant.

The Dot-Com Bubble (The Telecom Crash of 2000–2002)

All the fiber-optic cable! 39 million miles! Dark fiber...

Telecom companies took on massive amounts of debt to lay fiber-optic cable under oceans and across continents. Famous bankruptcies included Global Crossing, WorldCom, 360networks, and AboveNet. Worldwide telecommunications debt was estimated at $1 trillion.

By April 2001, utilization of the long-distance backbone had fallen below 3%. By 2004, bandwidth prices had fallen by more than 90%.

Companies like Google, Amazon, Netflix, and Facebook subsequently benefited from that ridiculously inexpensive bandwidth, making data-intensive services like streaming video, social media, and cloud computing economically viable.

The Internet bubble burst. The Internet did not become irrelevant.

The AI Bubble (The Current GPU and Data Center Buildout)All the data centers! All the GPUs! Dark compute...

CoreWeave alone has $47.5 billion in debt. Venture-backed AI startups are burning through VC cash. Billions of dollars in AI hardware are being purchased ahead of the electrical infrastructure necessary to operate it. Power grids, transformers, and substations cannot keep pace.

If the bubble bursts, who inherits the infrastructure?The better-capitalized hyperscalers, surviving AI companies, and potentially entirely new businesses.

But perhaps the biggest beneficiaries will be the non-tech Fortune 500 companies: banks, logistics networks, healthcare providers, manufacturers, and retailers. As the cost of compute collapses, they will be able to integrate AI into their existing systems and pursue actual productivity gains, much as businesses eventually embraced the Internet when bandwidth became inexpensive.

GPUs admittedly have a shorter economic lifespan than railroad tracks or fiber-optic cables. But the data centers, electrical infrastructure, cooling systems, and networking infrastructure will remain.

#9916. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

The lexical fallback for scale-to-zero and the separate index activation boundary are useful production details. One question for the hybrid setup: do you measure relevance and latency separately when dense search is cold versus warm, so fallback quality is visible rather than hidden in an overall average? We examined lexical-first retrieval and semantic reranking on a smaller workload here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That benchmark doesn't establish behavior on a paper-scale corpus.

#9915. AWS adds virtual iPhones to its cloud

Emulating Android, too, but offers just two handsets and one tablet

AWS now offers two new types of cloudy computers: emulated Androids and simulated iPhones.

The cloudy colossus announced both virtual offerings on Wednesday. They’re part of its Device Farm service, which previously saw AWS offer developers the chance to test their software on actual iOS and Android devices that reside in the Amazonian cloud. AWS will now also host virtual devices running Android and iOS.

AWS touts the virtual mobile devices as superior to physical devices.

“With virtual devices, you can shift testing left to stages that need high speed and volume, such as pull requests, code merges, and smoke tests, and keep real devices for later stages that need high fidelity, such as regression and release testing,” the cloudy business unit argues in its launch announcement.

AWS also says developers can get to work faster on a virtual iPhone or Pixel. “Virtual devices running the latest device and OS typically start in seconds, and others start in around a minute,” the outfit argues.

That may sound appetizing, but Amazon’s menu of virtual devices is short and bland.

When The Register logged on as an AWS user, the only emulated Android phone listed was a Google Pixel 10, running Android 15, 16, or 17. An emulated Pixel tablet running Android 17 is also on the menu.

At the time of writing, we could find only a virtual iPhone 16, running iOS 18.6, 23.61, and 27.0.

Analyst firm Counterpoint’s list of the world’s top 10 best-selling smartphones in Q2 of 2026 does not include a single Pixel device. The iPhone 16 occupies 10th place.

iPhone 17 models occupy the first, second, third, and seventh place on the list.

AWS might excite more developers if it adds emulators for the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy A07 4G, A17 5G, A17 4G, and Galaxy S26, as they occupy the fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth and ninth places on Counterpoint’s list.

Amazon’s choice of a Pixel tablet is also an oddity given analyst firm IDC doesn’t list Google among its top five tablet vendors.

Amazon does offer physical Galaxy A17 devices and three versions of the iPhone 17. But Device Farm doesn’t offer any foldable devices, meaning developers struggling to wrap their heads around the iPhone Duo will need either ask Apple for a loaner or shell out $2,000 to acquire one.

At least developers don’t have to change behavior to access the few virtual devices AWS offers, as existing Device Farm APIs and test frameworks will work on real or notional machines. ®

#9914. The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language

published: June 21, 2026 - last updated: November 27, 2026

Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving (opens new window), and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.

Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens new window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window). The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.

But that's easier said than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens new window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.

It might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:

Proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.

This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.

My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.

I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window):

So now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:

This design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.

A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is Deno (opens new window): Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a runtime layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.

I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the Magmide repo (opens new window) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification must become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.

And you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that doesn't happen (opens new window), history will look back on us even more foolish and disastrous than all the millennialists (opens new window) who merely wasted their own time and resources.

It is our responsibility to meet the challenges of our age with full agency and responsibility, and treat the emergence of a beneficent super-intelligence as an improbable jackpot.

#9913. Wire It, Run It, Deploy It: AI Workflows in Gradio

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

One graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

Every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:

The fastest way in is to open any demo above, click Duplicate, and start rewiring. From Python, it is as short as:

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

You can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇

Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.

This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.

What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

Smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up issues, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next plan starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

Take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

You don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count says you are.

We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”

#9911. Proof automation in a language

As I wrote previously, we have proof automation now. Given that fact, I think a very timely question is: how can we use it to improve software quality? The same machines that can write these proofs can also write large amounts of code. So an adjacent question is: how can we use them to improve software understandability?

It would be a mistake to start off afresh on those problems because there have been a lot of ideas in programming language design over the decades. The viability of ideas shifts as the underlying cost structures change, so things that didn't take off at the time might suddenly make a lot more sense. Still, language design involves a lot of tradeoffs, and features sometimes interact in surprising ways, so a lot of the work involves mixing some interesting-seeming ingredients together, baking, and asking “what is this? Is this a cake?”.

So I wanted to give a taste of some of the ingredients that I'm thinking about at the moment, and of the result.

Value semantics roughly says that you can't observe mutations to one variable through a different name. Value semantics are great for reasoning locally about code as, without them, you're constantly unsure what non-local effects might be happening.

When you work in a language, you instinctively know when it's using value semantics and when it's using reference semantics. Take Python:

You likely know that that prints [2]. (Although if you write the same program in C++ with std::vector it prints [1]! There's no cross-language norm for this.)

Over the span of four lines of code, this is irrelevant. But as the scope of the sharing increases, so does the mental complexity. If you want to be able to jump into a bit of code and understand what it's doing, knowing that there is no such aliasing is a huge boon.

Functional programming resolves this by eliminating mutation: if there's no mutation then you certainly can't observe mutations via a different variable name. But mutation is important for efficiency and a lot of work is then required to get the efficiency back. Lean, for example, will do in-place mutations if there's only a single reference to an object. That's great! But it has the sharp edge that innocent-looking changes can mean that there's now a hidden reference kept somewhere and performance crashes.

Rust claims to fix both issues by restricting references so that you can't ever have both a mutable reference to something, and an active alias to it. (We'll ignore Rc> and friends.)

Certainly Rust's restrictions help a great deal, but Mutable Value Semantics says that Rust goes too far by making references first-class, i.e. something that you can return and store in structures. First-class references lead to the borrow checker, which has undergone several deep rewrites (original to NLL, next to Polonius) to try and perfect it, and they lead to lifetimes, DerefMut etc., and much more complexity in the type system in general.

So an MVS system avoids all that by further restricting references and not allowing them in the type system. These ideas started in Swift and are currently championed in Hylo. The best introduction I've found is this talk.

In an MVS system, functions can take three sorts of arguments: immutable, mutable, and owned. Immutable arguments might be a reference or a copy; the semantics are the same. Mutable arguments are conceptually copied in at call time and copied back out when a function returns, but of course that's semantically the same as taking a pointer. Lastly, owned arguments transfer ownership to the function and make it unusable in the caller afterwards.

But there are no references in the type system, so a function can't return or store them. But the inability to return references implies so much copying that MVS systems need to provide an alternative.

Hylo has a very cute system of scoped coroutines, inspired by Swift. These coroutines yield a value and, at the call site, all their arguments are locked for the duration of that value's span. At the end of the span, the coroutine continues running.

One of the common examples is that a coroutine can return a mutable bool for a vector of bits that have been packed into bytes. Then, when the coroutine continues once the return value is no longer used, it can write the new value of that bool back into the array of bytes. This wouldn't be possible without a coroutine because the function would have to return a pointer to a bool that exists nowhere in memory.

Having just lionised this feature, I should note that in my experiments I haven't actually included it because it makes the semantics more complex and I'm spending a lot of complexity budget on verification instead. Which brings us to another idea that combines with MVS…

If you want to do formal verification on a language like C, then you need to model the heap and you immediately hit the aliasing issues above. Then you end up with a separation logic which lets you model disjoint areas of the heap (i.e. areas with no aliasing between them). Once you can speak about independent heaps, you can reason about a function that operates on one heap and hold the remainder constant.

This can work. The example that I'm (passingly) familiar with is the Verified Software Toolchain which connects to CompCert's semantics and allows you to state properties about C programs (with a separation logic) and thus verify C code all the way to machine code. But it's complex.

However! If you have restricted references then you can drop a huge amount of complexity from such systems! Aeneas/Charon is the current canonical example of this which can translate a subset of Rust code into Lean (and other languages) where things can then be proved about it. Because of Rust's restrictions, the translation doesn't need a separation logic.

But by being more restrictive than Rust, MVS languages are even more amenable to such translation, and thus to formal verification, without going all the way to being functional languages and banning mutation completely.

Eiffel is the standard reference here. It introduced preconditions, postconditions, and invariants for functions/classes:

While you've probably never used Eiffel, these notions are quite widespread now, although in common programming languages they are at best encoded in assertions if simple, comments if not, but mostly remain only in the author's head.

Eiffel did all its checks at run-time. There has been a lot of work on the balance between run-time and compile-time for these assertions, and on how to discharge assertions statically. Briefly, some work in this space that I'm aware of:

Dafny allows a mixture of run-time and static assertions, and discharges the static ones via SMT solvers. F* does everything statically, again using SMT solvers, but with a functional language. SPARK has a mixture of run-time and static checks, using SMT solvers or (albeit very challenging to use) provers via Why3. I've never touched Verus but it's worth a mention because it's the most recent entry in this lineage and is Rust-based.

The problem with these systems is that the compile-time checking is much more powerful, because it can cover all possible values of the arguments, but the proof burden is significant. SMT solvers help a lot, but they can quickly hit (effective) non-termination for non-trivial cases. I did an F* summer school in Paris once, and the experienced people there had developed a sixth sense about what would displease the SMT solver and would instinctively code around it. It was an impressive skill! But not reassuring.

This is the key cost that has changed: SMT solvers were inadequate for more complex cases, and dropping into a proof assistant overwhelmed you with lots of inscrutable proof states. All this can be largely handled by models now.

Also, I claim that there are some interesting synergies between MVS and design-by-contract. In Rust, and more so in an MVS system, you end up using indices into arenas of objects to replace arbitrary pointers. (Which can be faster due to cache locality.)

Given that one has all these indices flying around, wouldn't it be nice to have explicit invariants about them? Hopefully proven?

When writing code I will fairly often have some structure which has invariants that update as processing progresses. At some early part of the pipeline, the structure may be relatively arbitrary, perhaps freshly parsed from a file, and then as various checks and transforms are applied we know more and more about the value.

But in traditional languages, the structure has one type: its structural type. Even with Eiffel-style Design by Contract, invariants on a type are fixed.

The idea of being able to attach more invariants to a structure without duplicating most of it showed up as Subtypes in proof systems, and refinement types in ML. You'll also see Rust code do this (mostly at run-time) with checked constructors like NonZero and NonNull. But those are run-time checks that the type system carries a certificate of. Similar to the evolution of Eiffel-style conditions, we can hope to make them static checks now, discharged via our new proof automation.

Literate programming was the title of a paper by Knuth in the 80s, and WEB was the original implementation. The idea is that code should be written to be read and thus that it should be ordered for human, not machine, consumption, and that exposition should be at least as important as the code, and not relegated to comments.

Nearly twenty years ago I wanted to understand critbit trees and so wrote an implementation using CWEB to explore both ideas.

Relatedly, in my mind code has a graph structure deriving from which functions call which other functions. Source files are groups of strongly connected functions and I generally have little memory for what order functions have in a given source file. With the widespread use of LSPs and thus code indexing, we are edging slowly towards being less file orientated but I still feel that we could do much more.

There was a burst of such ideas in the 80s: Knuth's work, also Smalltalk & Lisp systems which kept code in databases rather than text files. Given the ecosystem of version control that assumes text-based files, code databases might be too awkward now, but I still feel the itch of dissatisfaction here.

At the top of this post I also set a goal for code to be more understandable and, to that end, the easiest code to understand is the code that you didn't have to read because the contract says all that you need to know about it.

Here's a function that looks like Rust (because I don't have better syntax ideas) but which doesn't verify.

When I'm reading code, I'm always trying to track the invariants and think about integer overflows. Sometimes the codebase aims to be overflow-clean and so I'm following bounds precisely. Most of the time I just have to ignore them unless the overflow is especially egregious. Now that we have proof automation, I shouldn't have to do that. So, as in SPARK, Verus, and others, + must statically not overflow and compiling the above gets you:

That's the SMT solver giving you a counterexample that overflows. (+%, as in Zig, exists if you really want wrapping operations.)

If the values are bounded such that overflow can't happen, then obviously everything will be fine, automatically:

Casts are similar: u32::from is safe because it must be widening. For narrowing, u32::exact_from statically requires that the cast not truncate and, if you really need the machine operation, u32::wrap_from gives it to you.

And, of course, all vector indices must be statically valid.

Let me try and convince you of the benefits of contracts in terms of code understandability. For this, we're going to discuss a tiny bit of DER, the most common ASN.1 encoding.

DER is a tag-length-value format. We're just going to talk about the encoding of tags. Firstly, tags are in one of four classes which have integer values on the wire:

A DER tag is then a class and a tag number, plus a flag which tells you whether the value contains more DER values nested inside it. In theory, tag numbers are unbounded integers. In practice, everyone limits them; here we'll bound them below 228 because, as you'll see, that limits the tags to five bytes and the next byte would exceed 232. The (class, tag number) combination of (Universal, 0) is banned in DER as it's the BER end-of-contents value:

A tag can be encoded as one or more bytes. The first byte has two bits of class, one bit for the constructed flag, and five bits of tag number. If the tag number is ≥ 0x1f (the maximum 5-bit value) then it's encoded as 0x1f and more bytes of tag follow:

The tag numbers that need more bytes are big-endian, base-128 encoded, with the high bit set each time if another byte follows:

Now, here's an encoding function for DER tags:

The body of the function is missing—but you don't need it! The contract requires that it encodes exactly as tag_enc specifies so you don't need to know more. This isn't saving you too much because the code isn't that complicated. You would have to think about the shifts and masks that it's using for the base-128 encoding (rather than recursion), but that's only a few seconds.

This enforces not just the baseline of memory safety, no run-time panics etc., but that the parser is fully strict: it never parses anything other than the canonical encoding of a value, as defined above. This is not a trivial thing to code review, and here you don't have to.

Also you see signs of MVS: a Reader can't hold a reference to in because references can't be stored. Thus in is passed separately (and the indices are proven to be valid). This is part of the tradeoff for local reasoning and strong contracts.

I've not mentioned linear types, views in return values, or Zig-style error unions, and I'll only touch on refinement types in the lightest sense by noting the pleasing definition of the String type in this experiment:

Lastly, nodding towards literate programming, I'll note that this blog post itself is a valid source file for this language: the language consumes Markdown files and only compiles lines in annotated code blocks. The Lean proofs are kept in separate files, not for human consumption. There's already a tool for showing a source file with only the public definitions, and with the bodies of functions elided, and there's still more I want to explore here in terms of viewing source files as a graph.

It's worth discussing the more bitter flavours in this cake too.

The front end of the compiler emits lots of verification conditions for the code to be correct. Every arithmetic operation emits overflow checks, every indexing operation emits range checks, every invariant and postcondition results in checks, every loop must be shown to be terminating, etc.

The little DER tag example above results in 149 of them. Each is first sent to Z3 and then, if Z3 times out (after a couple of seconds), to cvc5. But the solvers are never trusted. If they believe that a condition holds they output the unsat core which is used to trim the hypotheses which are fed into Lean. Lean automation chews on the problem for a while and, if that times out, an LLM comes to write a manual proof in Lean.

There's a cache of proven conditions, of course, and the Lean proofs are saved in a different file. But overall even reasonably simple examples type-check at about 10 lines per second. If you invalidate the cache then medium-sized programs can take multiple hours to recheck on a fast machine. (Not reprove, just to check the proofs that already exist!) So modularity of code is important to keep the scaling line flatter.

LLM compute is needed too: after I laid out the spec for the DER tag example above, a model took about 30 minutes to get it working. But if you ask a modern model to write the same thing in Go, it will do it in under 10 seconds. (Although the result doesn't hit nearly the same quality bar and the lax parsing would cause security problems in sensitive contexts.)

Overall, this language was an experiment in how we can convert compute into high-quality and understandable code. I'll claim that it's making interesting steps towards that goal, but you do need a lot of compute.

Also, there is a considerable trusted base involved here. While you don't have to trust the SMT solvers, you do have to trust that the front end is correctly translating the code into verification conditions for Lean, and you have to trust that it is correctly translating it into LLVM IR. I think that's fine: the comparison here is with regular languages like C++ and Rust. This is not an attempt at a minimal TCB language with extremely strong guarantees like CakeML.

Still, the language does have significant aspects of delight. Being able to write the spec for DER encoding, and then have the correct code for it generated, does make me reflect on the amount of time and suffering that I've put into DER over the years that could now be avoided.

Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know.

Editor’s note (November 17, 2026): This post has been updated with additional CVE information and updated guidance for GitHub Enterprise Server users. Please see the release information below for the versions that include the fixes.

Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.An attacker-controlled Git server can exploit this discrepancy to replace a clone’s .git file or directory, redirecting Git to attacker-controlled configuration or hooks.For recursive clones, this can execute attacker-controlled code during the clone. For non-recursive clones, an attacker can replace the top-level .git directory with a file pointing to attacker-controlled repository metadata. The clone can then report an error and recommend running git status in the resulting directory; following that advice can execute attacker-controlled code.The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Robert Chen reported CVE-2026-111760, which was fixed by Elijah Newren and Toon Claes, with help from Johannes Schindelin and Jeff King. Luke Martin reported CVE-2026-113408, which was fixed by Toon Claes.

pwn2addr reported CVE-2026-114466, CVE-2026-114467, and CVE-2026-114469, which were fixed by Karthik Nayak. Kaartic Sivaraam implemented the fix for CVE-2026-105437 based on a patch by Jeff King, with help from Toon Claes and Christian Couder.

Elijah Newren is a Staff Software Engineer at GitHub. He is the designer and implementer of merge-ort, Git's default merge strategy since 2.34, author of git-filter-repo—the history rewriting tool the Git project officially recommends—and a driving force behind sparse-checkout.

#9908. Support team put in an emergency order for vodka – lots of vodka – to bring PCs back online

The end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early. Friday mornings bring a new installment of On Call – the column in which we share your stories of doing whatever it takes to keep tech running.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station.

"We used to have about 30 PCs, all running slightly different radio shows depending on the time zone where we broadcast," he explained.

The PCs were old clunkers running Windows 95 long after Microsoft ended support for the OS. Management knew the machines needed replacing, but funding was probably another year away.

"We had to coax them on till then," Bruce wrote. "And by coax, I mean we were buying RAM on eBay because nobody sold the 4MB sticks we needed anymore."

Thanks to the tender ministrations of Bruce and his colleagues, the PCs kept humming and the radio stations stayed on the air.

Until a lovely spring Tuesday, when Bruce and his crew enjoyed a bucolic cup of tea in the first real sunshine of the season and received a call informing them that one of the stations was down.

One of Bruce's mates figured a cranky old PC probably just needed a reboot and headed off to fix it while the rest of the team enjoyed their tea.

And then the phone rang again to report another outage, so Bruce and the entire crew went back to work, chatting about which switch or other shared device could have taken out two PCs.

When they arrived in the office, the chap who had gone to reboot the first PC ran in and announced that the computer room had flooded.

Bruce and his teammates ran into that room and found dirty brown water all over the floor, walls, ceiling, and the racks holding the ancient PCs.

"Water was even spraying out of the front fans of the last two PCs that were still working," Bruce told The Register.

"After a lot of shouting words unfit to print, we all got to work ripping them out, shutting down what we could that looked to be working, and started lining them up outside in the car park," Bruce wrote. "Some of us then got to work stripping them down into component parts, others washed them down with isopropanol."

As the isopropanol supply dwindled, one of the team arranged an urgent delivery of vodka.

"Luckily, it was a gloriously sunny day, so we quickly rinsed the PCs and left them to dry, strewn all over the car park," Bruce wrote.

By this stage, he and the team were all filthy and exhausted. With the stations still offline, they had to rebuild the PCs and get them running again.

"We only lost two sticks of RAM, one sound card, and a power supply," Bruce wrote.

The culprit turned out to be a new hire on the facilities team who, while touring the building, had turned a random tap to see what would happen.

"It released water from a stagnant iron tank that sat there rusting away for years," Bruce wrote. For reasons nobody understood, the tank drained through a pipe into the room housing the broadcast PCs.

Have you had to clean up hardware in a hurry, perhaps with odd substances or implements? If so, click here to send On Call your story. We'll raise a glass to each one of you who sends a story and do it again if we share it on a future Friday. ®
